prompt: What is new in C++20 and C++23?
completion:
Below is a “high‑level” snapshot of what really changed between the previous standard (C++17) and the two most recent releases, C++20 and C++23.  
The list is intentionally selective – it focuses on the big, language‑wide or library‑wide items that developers actually notice when upgrading their code bases. (For the complete technical specification, see the ISO C++ Standard documents or the exhaustive “What’s New” pages on cppreference.com.)

---

## C++20 – the “big‑bang” release

| Category | New feature | Why it matters | Example |
|----------|-------------|----------------|---------|
| **Language** | **Modules** | Replaces the fragile header‑based include system with a first‑class module system (precompiled units, no header‑surgery). | `export module mylib; export void f();` |
| | **Concepts** | Compile‑time predicates that enable readable constraints and better error messages. | `template <typename T> concept Integral = std::is_integral_v<T>;` |
| | **Three‑way comparison** (`<=>`) | Unified equality/ordering, generates `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`. | `auto res = a <=> b;` |
| | **Coroutines** (`co_await`, `co_yield`, `co_return`) | Simplifies async and generator code. | `co_return 42;` |
| | **`consteval` & `constinit`** | Forces compile‑time evaluation or guarantees constant initialization. | `consteval int factorial(int n) { … }` |
| | **`constexpr` improvements** | `constexpr` now supports virtual functions, dynamic allocations (in C++20, `std::vector`), `try`/`catch`, etc. | `constexpr std::vector<int> v = {1,2,3};` |
| | **`[[likely]]`, `[[unlikely]]`, `[[nodiscard]]`, `[[no_unique_address]]`** | Better optimizer hints, safety. | `int [[nodiscard]] foo();` |
| | **`std::bit_cast` (P0135R1)** | Safe reinterpretation of bit patterns. | `std::bit_cast<float>(0x40490fdb);` |
| | **`std::from_chars` for `std::chrono` types** | Low‑overhead conversion of strings to time points / durations. | `std::from_chars("2021-12-31", std::chrono::year_month_day{});` |
| | **`std::span`** | Non‑owning view of contiguous sequences. | `std::span<int> s(arr, 5);` |
| | **`std::ranges`** | View adapters and algorithms that work lazily. | `std::ranges::sort(vec);` |
| | **`std::format` (P0962)** | Type‑safe, C++‑style printf/formatting. | `std::format("pi ≈ {:.2f}", 3.14159);` |
| | **`std::execution` policy for parallel algorithms** | Parallelism with `std::sort(par, …)` etc. | `std::sort(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end());` |
| | **`std::optional`, `std::variant`, `std::any`, `std::string_view`, `std::filesystem`** | Brought to the language from earlier proposals; now fully standard. | `std::optional<int> opt = 5;` |
| | **`std::scoped_lock`, `std::latch`, `std::barrier`** | New concurrency primitives. | `std::latch l(3);` |
| | **`std::bitset`, `std::array` constexpr** | More compile‑time utilities. | `constexpr std::array<int, 3> arr = {1,2,3};` |
| | **`[[nodiscard]]` and `[[maybe_unused]]` improvements** | Better diagnostics. | `[[nodiscard]] int f();` |
| | **`std::expected` was *not* in C++20** – it arrives in C++23 (see below). |

---

## C++23 – the “incremental but important” release

C++23 builds on top of C++20 and finalises a number of proposals that were only in draft at the time of C++20.  The most visible changes are library‑wide; the language itself still has only a handful of new keywords (mostly `consteval`, `constinit`, `requires` already existed in C++20).  

| Category | New feature | Why it matters | Example |
|----------|-------------|----------------|---------|
| **Library – error handling** | **`std::expected<T, E>`** | A type that represents either a value (`T`) or an error (`E`), similar to `Result` in Rust or `Option`+`Err` in Swift. | `std::expected<int, std::string> res = parse_int(s);` |
| | **`std::span` improvements** | Multi‑dimensional views (`std::span<std::span<int>>`), `subspan`, and non‑char overloads. | `std::span<int> row = matrix[i].data();` |
| | **`std::to_array`** | Compile‑time creation of `std::array` from an initializer list. | `auto a = std::to_array({1,2,3});` |
| | **`std::erase` / `std::erase_if`** | Algorithms that remove elements from containers in a single call. | `std::erase_if(v, [](int x){ return x<0; });` |
| | **`std::ranges::to`** | Convert a range into a container (`auto v = std::ranges::to<std::vector>(range);`). | `auto v = std::ranges::to<std::vector>(view);` |
| | **`std::bit_cast` finalised** | Already a draft in C++20, now fully standardised. | `auto f = std::bit_cast<float>(0x3f800000);` |
| | **`std::unreachable`** | Signal that a branch is unreachable (hint to optimizer). | `if (cond) { … } else std::unreachable();` |
| | **`std::from_chars` for floating‑point types** | Low‑level parsing for `double`, `long double`. | `std::from_chars("3.14", 0, 0, std::to_chars_result);` |
| | **`std::is_constant_evaluated()`** | Detect if a function is running in constant evaluation. | `if (std::is_constant_evaluated()) return 0;` |
| | **`std::expected` also gets `and_then`/`or_else`** | Chain operations on `expected` more ergonomically. | `auto res = opt.and_then([](int x){ return x*2; });` |
| | **`std::expected`'s `value_or`** | Get the contained value or a fallback. | `auto n = e.value_or(0);` |
| | **`std::span::data()` overload for `char16_t`/`char32_t`** | More type‑safe string views. | `std::span<char16_t> s16 = u"hello";` |
| | **`std::execution::par_unseq`** | Parallel and vectorised execution policy. | `std::sort(std::execution::par_unseq, v.begin(), v.end());` |
| | **`std::to_chars` improvements** | Support for many numeric types (`uint64_t`, `long double`). | `std::to_chars(buf, buf+10, 123456);` |
| | **`std::string_view::contains` & `starts_with` / `ends_with`** | More convenient string view operations. | `sv.contains("abc");` |
| | **`std::array`’s `std::array::fill`** | Simplified filling of `std::array`. | `arr.fill(0);` |
| | **`std::format` finalised** | The formatting library is now fully standard (already available in C++20, but finalised here). | `std::format("value={:08x}", 42);` |
| | **`std::format` for binary, hexadecimal, and scientific notation** | Richer formatting options. | `std::format("{:b}", 10);` |
| | **`std::format` `fmt::formatter` customization points** | Easy to extend formatting for user types. | `template<> struct fmt::formatter<MyType> { … };` |
| | **`std::expected`’s `transform`** | Transform the contained value. | `auto new_exp = exp.transform([](int x){ return x+1; });` |
| | **`std::expected`'s `match`** | Pattern‑matching style. | `exp.match([](int v){ … }, [](auto e){ … });` |
| | **`std::bit_cast` for non-trivially copyable types** | (C++23 allows this for trivially copyable types only, so no change here). | – |
| | **`std::vector` now supports `std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator` in the header** | (C++20 already had it, but C++23 finalises the implementation). | `std::pmr::vector<int> v;` |

---

### Deprecations / removals

| Feature | Status |
|---------|--------|
| `std::tr1` namespace | Removed |
| `std::auto_ptr` | Removed |
| `std::thread::get_id` overloads for `native_handle()` | Deprecated (C++17) |
| `std::valarray` heavy use | No longer recommended (but still present) |
| `std::ptrdiff_t` overloads for `std::distance`? | – |
| `std::complex<float>` in `<complex>` for `real`, `imag`? | – |

(If you’re maintaining legacy code, you’ll want to look at the “Deprecated and Removed” tables in the standard.)

## How to get started

1. **Compiler support**  
   - GCC 10+ (C++20), GCC 11+ (C++23)  
   - Clang 11+ (C++20), Clang 13+ (C++23)  
   - MSVC 19.28+ (C++20), MSVC 19.30+ (C++23)  
   (All modern compilers now fully support the core C++20 features and are largely C++23‑ready.)

2. **Toolchains & libraries**  
   - `libstdc++` 10+ (C++20) / 12+ (C++23)  
   - `libc++` 10+ (C++20) / 13+ (C++23)  
   - `MSVC` STL includes all features.  
   - `libc++` (Apple Clang) includes `std::expected` from 2023.

3. **Migration checklist**  
   - Replace all `std::auto_ptr` with `std::unique_ptr`.  
   - Add concepts to your template constraints for clearer error messages.  
   - Refactor manual loops into ranges where it makes sense (`std::ranges::views::filter`, `transform`, `for_each`).  
   - Move any heavy header dependencies into modules if you can.  
   - Use `std::expected` for error‑propagating functions instead of `throw`/`catch` if you want value‑based error handling.  
   - Replace manual `erase_if` loops with the new `std::erase_if` algorithm.  
   - If you’re doing a lot of string formatting, migrate to `std::format` to avoid external libs.  
   - Consider `std::span` for non‑owning buffer views to replace raw pointers.  

---

## Bottom line

* **C++20** is the “big‑feature” jump: concepts, modules, ranges, coroutines, three‑way comparison, constexpr overhauls, and the first stable `std::format`.  
* **C++23** is a *polish‑up* release that finalises many draft features, adds a few new convenient algorithms (`erase`, `to_array`, `ranges::to`), introduces `std::expected` for error handling, and brings in a handful of missing library pieces (`std::bit_cast`, `std::unreachable`, floating‑point `from_chars`).  

Together, they give you a powerful toolbox for modern C++ programming: safer, more expressive code with less boilerplate, and a standard library that is closer to what developers actually need in real projects.
